# Case Study Overview

**Problem.** An e-commerce website records every visitor session: which pages were
opened, how long the visitor stayed, and whether they left quickly. Most sessions do
not end in a purchase. The business wants to know which session behaviours are
associated with buying, and whether a simple model can predict if a session will end
in a purchase.

**Background.** Every visit leaves behavioural clues such as product pages viewed, time
spent, bounce and exit rates, visitor type and month. Data science can turn these
clues into patterns and a yes/no purchase prediction that helps a business improve its
pages and plan offers.

**Objectives**

1. Analyze online shopper session behaviour using the dataset.
2. Identify behavioural factors associated with purchase completion.
3. Visualize patterns between session characteristics and the purchase outcome.
4. Develop and evaluate a Logistic Regression model that predicts whether a session results in a purchase.

**What we predict.** The target is `Revenue`: `TRUE` if the session ended in a purchase,
`FALSE` otherwise. It is a yes/no (binary) outcome, not an amount of money.

# Dataset

```{r load-data}
# Step 2: Read the dataset.
# The CSV must be in the SAME folder as this .Rmd file.
# (The original script used choose.files(), which opens a pop-up window and
#  cannot run while knitting, so a fixed file name is used here.)
data_file <- "online_shoppers_intention.csv"
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  stop("Cannot find '", data_file, "'. Put the CSV in the same folder as this .Rmd file.")
}
data <- read.csv(data_file)
```

* **Name:** Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset
* **Source:** UCI Machine Learning Repository (Sakar & Kastro, 2018), <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5F88Q>
* **Size:** `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` sessions (rows) and `r ncol(data)` variables (columns). One row is one shopping session.
* **Target:** `Revenue` (purchase made: TRUE / FALSE)

**Why it suits this case study:** it records real online shopping sessions, contains
behavioural variables, and its target directly records whether a purchase happened.
That makes it suitable for both behaviour analysis and binary purchase prediction.

```{r inspect}
# Step 3: Inspect the dataset (size, first rows, variable types).
dim(data)
head(data[, 1:9])   # first 9 columns (all 18 do not fit on one line)

# A compact table of every variable and its type as read by R
data.frame(
  Variable = names(data),
  R_type   = vapply(data, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1)),
  Example  = vapply(data, function(x) as.character(x[1]), character(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

**Important variables.** `Administrative`, `Informational` and `ProductRelated` count the
pages of each type viewed, and their `_Duration` columns give the time spent on them.
`BounceRates`, `ExitRates` and `PageValues` are Google Analytics measures for the pages
visited. `SpecialDay` measures closeness to a special day such as Valentine's Day.
`Month`, `VisitorType` and `Weekend` describe when and by whom the visit was made.
`OperatingSystems`, `Browser`, `Region` and `TrafficType` are stored as numbers but are
really category codes.

# Data Preparation

## Missing values

```{r missing}
# Step 4: Check missing values in every column.
colSums(is.na(data))
```

The dataset has **`r sum(is.na(data))` missing values**, which matches the information on
the UCI page. No imputation is needed.

## Duplicate rows

```{r duplicates}
# Step 5: Count duplicate rows (rows identical in all 18 columns).
sum(duplicated(data))

# Step 6: Inspect the duplicate rows.
duplicate_rows <- data[duplicated(data), ]
head(duplicate_rows[, c("ProductRelated", "ProductRelated_Duration",
                        "BounceRates", "ExitRates", "PageValues", "Revenue")])

# Purchase outcome among the duplicate rows
table(duplicate_rows$Revenue)

# How many duplicates are very short "bounce" sessions?
# (bounce rate and exit rate both 0.2, at most 1 product page, 0 seconds on product pages)
sum(duplicate_rows$BounceRates == 0.2 & duplicate_rows$ExitRates == 0.2 &
    duplicate_rows$ProductRelated <= 1 & duplicate_rows$ProductRelated_Duration == 0)
```

**Decision: duplicates are kept, not removed.** There are `r sum(duplicated(data))`
duplicate rows. All of them are non-purchase sessions with bounce and exit rate 0.2,
and almost all are one-page visits with no time recorded. UCI states that each
session belongs to a different user. So these rows most likely are *different* visitors
whose very short visits happened to produce identical values, not copying errors.
Removing them would hide real (and common) quick-exit behaviour. Section 5.8 checks
that keeping them does not change the conclusions.

## Numerical variables and value ranges

```{r ranges}
# Step 7: Summary of numerical variables (minimum, median, mean, maximum).
numeric_vars <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.numeric)]
numeric_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = numeric_vars,
  Min    = sapply(data[numeric_vars], min),
  Median = sapply(data[numeric_vars], median),
  Mean   = round(sapply(data[numeric_vars], mean), 2),
  Max    = sapply(data[numeric_vars], max),
  row.names = NULL
)
numeric_summary

# Check that the rates are inside their valid range (0 to 1)
range(data$BounceRates)
range(data$ExitRates)
range(data$PageValues)
# Durations and page counts should never be negative
any(data[, c("Administrative_Duration", "Informational_Duration",
             "ProductRelated_Duration")] < 0)
```

No incorrect values were found: bounce and exit rates lie between 0 and 1, and no
duration is negative. Several variables (durations, `PageValues`) are strongly
**right-skewed**: most sessions have small values and a few have very large values.
These large values are plausible (for example, a long shopping session), so they are
kept as they are, and no transformation was applied.

## Converting categorical variables to factors

```{r factors}
# Step 8: Convert categorical variables to factors.
# OperatingSystems, Browser, Region and TrafficType are number CODES (labels),
# not quantities, so R must treat them as categories.
data$OperatingSystems <- as.factor(data$OperatingSystems)
data$Browser          <- as.factor(data$Browser)
data$Region           <- as.factor(data$Region)
data$TrafficType      <- as.factor(data$TrafficType)

data$Month       <- as.factor(data$Month)
data$VisitorType <- as.factor(data$VisitorType)
data$Weekend     <- as.factor(data$Weekend)
data$Revenue     <- as.factor(data$Revenue)   # target: levels "FALSE", "TRUE"

# Verify the updated data types
str(data)
```

Note: `Month` has only `r nlevels(data$Month)` levels because the dataset contains
no January or April sessions. `June` is written in full while the other months are
abbreviated; this is how the data comes from UCI.

# Data Analysis and Visualization

## Purchase vs non-purchase sessions

```{r plot-revenue}
# Step 9: Purchase vs Non-Purchase Sessions
ggplot(data, aes(x = Revenue, fill = Revenue)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Purchase vs Non-Purchase Sessions",
    x = "Purchase Outcome",
    y = "Number of Sessions",
    fill = "Revenue"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Counts and percentages
revenue_table <- data %>%
  count(Revenue, name = "Sessions") %>%
  mutate(Percent = round(100 * Sessions / sum(Sessions), 2))
revenue_table
```

**Interpretation:** only `r revenue_table$Percent[revenue_table$Revenue == "TRUE"]`% of
sessions end in a purchase. The classes are **imbalanced**, so accuracy alone can be
misleading: a model that always predicts "no purchase" would already be about
`r round(revenue_table$Percent[revenue_table$Revenue == "FALSE"])`% accurate. That is why precision, recall and
F1-score are also reported in Section 5.

## Bounce rate and exit rate

```{r plot-bounce}
# Step 10A: Bounce Rate by Purchase Outcome
ggplot(data, aes(x = Revenue, y = BounceRates, fill = Revenue)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Bounce Rate by Purchase Outcome",
    x = "Purchase Outcome",
    y = "Bounce Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r plot-exit}
# Step 10B: Exit Rate by Purchase Outcome
ggplot(data, aes(x = Revenue, y = ExitRates, fill = Revenue)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Exit Rate by Purchase Outcome",
    x = "Purchase Outcome",
    y = "Exit Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Median and mean of each rate for the two groups
rate_summary <- data %>%
  group_by(Revenue) %>%
  summarise(
    Median_BounceRate = round(median(BounceRates), 4),
    Mean_BounceRate   = round(mean(BounceRates), 4),
    Median_ExitRate   = round(median(ExitRates), 4),
    Mean_ExitRate     = round(mean(ExitRates), 4)
  )
rate_summary
```

**Interpretation:** sessions that end in a purchase have clearly **lower bounce and exit
rates** (mean exit rate `r rate_summary$Mean_ExitRate[rate_summary$Revenue == "TRUE"]`
for purchases vs `r rate_summary$Mean_ExitRate[rate_summary$Revenue == "FALSE"]` for
non-purchases). The points above the boxes are sessions with unusually high rates.
At the maximum value of 0.2 (visitors who left almost immediately) there are
`r sum(data$BounceRates == 0.2 & data$Revenue == "FALSE")` non-purchase sessions but only
`r sum(data$BounceRates == 0.2 & data$Revenue == "TRUE")` purchase session(s).

## Purchase outcome by visitor type

```{r plot-visitor}
# Purchase outcome by visitor type (each bar adds up to 1)
ggplot(data, aes(x = VisitorType, fill = Revenue)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Outcome by Visitor Type",
    x = "Visitor Type",
    y = "Proportion of Sessions",
    fill = "Purchase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Step 21: Purchase proportion by visitor type
purchase_summary <- aggregate(
  I(Revenue == "TRUE") ~ VisitorType,
  data = data,
  FUN = mean
)
names(purchase_summary)[2] <- "Purchase_Proportion"
purchase_summary$Sessions <- as.vector(table(data$VisitorType)[purchase_summary$VisitorType])
purchase_summary$Purchase_Proportion <- round(purchase_summary$Purchase_Proportion, 4)
purchase_summary
```

**Interpretation:** new visitors buy in a larger share of their sessions
(`r round(100 * purchase_summary$Purchase_Proportion[purchase_summary$VisitorType == "New_Visitor"], 1)`%)
than returning visitors
(`r round(100 * purchase_summary$Purchase_Proportion[purchase_summary$VisitorType == "Returning_Visitor"], 1)`%),
although returning visitors make up most sessions. The "Other" group is very small
(`r purchase_summary$Sessions[purchase_summary$VisitorType == "Other"]` sessions), so its
proportion is less reliable.

## Purchase rate by month *(added)*

```{r plot-month}
# Months are re-ordered in calendar order for the chart only.
# (The model in Section 5 uses the original factor; this re-ordering does not affect it.)
month_order <- c("Feb", "Mar", "May", "June", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")

month_summary <- data %>%
  mutate(Month = factor(Month, levels = month_order)) %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(Sessions = n(),
            Purchase_Rate = round(mean(Revenue == "TRUE"), 4))

ggplot(month_summary, aes(x = Month, y = Purchase_Rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(100 * Purchase_Rate, 1), "%")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Purchase Rate by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Share of Sessions Ending in a Purchase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

month_summary
```

**Interpretation:** the purchase rate is highest in
**`r as.character(month_summary$Month[which.max(month_summary$Purchase_Rate)])`**
(`r round(100 * max(month_summary$Purchase_Rate), 1)`%) and lowest in
**`r as.character(month_summary$Month[which.min(month_summary$Purchase_Rate)])`**
(`r round(100 * min(month_summary$Purchase_Rate), 1)`%). The number of sessions also
differs a lot between months, so months with few sessions should be read with care.

## Correlation between numerical variables *(added)*

```{r plot-correlation, fig.height = 5.5}
# Correlation matrix of the 10 numerical variables
num_cols <- c("Administrative", "Administrative_Duration", "Informational",
              "Informational_Duration", "ProductRelated", "ProductRelated_Duration",
              "BounceRates", "ExitRates", "PageValues", "SpecialDay")
cor_matrix <- cor(data[, num_cols])

# Reshape the matrix into a long table (Var1, Var2, Correlation) for ggplot
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))
names(cor_long) <- c("Var1", "Var2", "Correlation")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 2)), size = 2.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Heatmap of Numerical Variables",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Interpretation:** each page count is strongly correlated with its own duration
(for example `ProductRelated` vs `ProductRelated_Duration`: r =
`r round(cor_matrix["ProductRelated", "ProductRelated_Duration"], 2)`), and
`BounceRates` is strongly correlated with `ExitRates` (r =
`r round(cor_matrix["BounceRates", "ExitRates"], 2)`). These pairs carry overlapping
information. Logistic Regression can still be fitted, but the individual
coefficients of correlated variables should be interpreted with care.

# Prediction / Model

## Method and why it is suitable

The target `Revenue` has two outcomes, so this is a **binary classification** problem.
**Logistic Regression** (`glm()` with `family = binomial`) is used because it:

* predicts the **probability** (0 to 1) that a session ends in a purchase;
* is a standard, well-understood method for yes/no targets;
* is simple and **interpretable**: each coefficient shows whether a variable raises or
  lowers the chance of purchase.

A probability is turned into a prediction using a **threshold**: if the probability is
at or above the threshold, the prediction is `TRUE` (purchase).

## Training and testing sets

```{r split}
# Step 11: Split data into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets.
# set.seed() makes the random split the same every time the report is knitted.
set.seed(123)

train_index <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(data)),
  size = floor(0.8 * nrow(data))
)

train_data <- data[train_index, ]
test_data  <- data[-train_index, ]

# Check the split
nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)

# Safety check: every Month level used by the model must appear in the training data,
# otherwise predict() would fail on the test data.
stopifnot(all(levels(data$Month) %in% unique(as.character(train_data$Month))))
```

## Model training

The model uses the 10 numerical behaviour variables plus `Month`, `VisitorType` and
`Weekend`, exactly as in the original script. `OperatingSystems`, `Browser`, `Region`
and `TrafficType` are **not** used: they are technical codes with many rare values
(some codes appear only once or twice), which can make `predict()` fail when a code
appears in the test set but not in the training set.

```{r model}
# Step 12: Train the Logistic Regression model on the TRAINING data only.
model <- glm(
  Revenue ~ Administrative +
    Administrative_Duration +
    Informational +
    Informational_Duration +
    ProductRelated +
    ProductRelated_Duration +
    BounceRates +
    ExitRates +
    PageValues +
    SpecialDay +
    Month +
    VisitorType +
    Weekend,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial
)

# Coefficient table (rounded).
# Odds_Ratio = exp(Estimate): above 1 raises the odds of purchase, below 1 lowers them.
coef_table <- as.data.frame(summary(model)$coefficients)
names(coef_table) <- c("Estimate", "Std_Error", "z_value", "p_value")
coef_table$Odds_Ratio  <- exp(coef_table$Estimate)
coef_table$Significant <- ifelse(coef_table$p_value < 0.05, "Yes (p < 0.05)", "No")
coef_table <- cbind(Term = rownames(coef_table), coef_table)
rownames(coef_table) <- NULL
coef_table[, 2:6] <- signif(coef_table[, 2:6], 4)
coef_table
```

**Interpretation:** the significant variables (p < 0.05) are
`r paste(setdiff(coef_table$Term[coef_table$p_value < 0.05], "(Intercept)"), collapse = ", ")`.
`PageValues` is a strong positive predictor: each 1-unit increase multiplies the odds
of purchase by about `r round(coef_table$Odds_Ratio[coef_table$Term == "PageValues"], 3)`.
`ExitRates` has a strong negative effect. Month coefficients are compared with the
reference month (`r levels(data$Month)[1]`, the first level alphabetically).

## Prediction on the test data

```{r predict}
# Step 13: Predict purchase probabilities for the TEST sessions.
probabilities <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = test_data,
  type = "response"
)

predictions <- ifelse(
  probabilities >= 0.5,
  "TRUE",
  "FALSE"
)

head(round(probabilities, 3), 10)
head(predictions, 10)
```

## Evaluation at the standard threshold 0.50

```{r evaluate-050}
# Step 14: Model Evaluation (threshold 0.50)

# Convert predictions and actual outcomes to factors with the same level order
predicted_class <- factor(predictions, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
actual_class    <- factor(test_data$Revenue, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))

# Create confusion matrix
confusion_matrix <- table(Actual = actual_class, Predicted = predicted_class)
print(confusion_matrix)

# Extract confusion matrix values
TN <- confusion_matrix["FALSE", "FALSE"]
FP <- confusion_matrix["FALSE", "TRUE"]
FN <- confusion_matrix["TRUE", "FALSE"]
TP <- confusion_matrix["TRUE", "TRUE"]

# Calculate evaluation metrics
accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(confusion_matrix)
precision <- ifelse(TP + FP == 0, 0, TP / (TP + FP))
recall    <- ifelse(TP + FN == 0, 0, TP / (TP + FN))
f1_score  <- ifelse(precision + recall == 0, 0,
                    2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall))

cat("Accuracy:",  round(accuracy  * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Precision:", round(precision * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Recall:",    round(recall    * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("F1-score:",  round(f1_score  * 100, 2), "%\n")
```

At 0.50 the model is accurate overall but finds only
`r round(100 * recall, 1)`% of the real purchases (`r TP` of `r TP + FN`).
Because purchases are rare, the predicted probabilities are usually low, and a 0.50
cut-off misses many buyers. A **lower threshold** catches more buyers.

## Choosing a lower threshold

To compare thresholds without repeating code, the same calculation as above is put
into one small function.

```{r metric-function}
# Same formulas as Step 14, wrapped in a function so they can be reused.
get_metrics <- function(probs, actual, threshold) {
  predicted <- factor(ifelse(probs >= threshold, "TRUE", "FALSE"), levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
  actual    <- factor(actual, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
  cm <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)
  TN <- cm["FALSE", "FALSE"]; FP <- cm["FALSE", "TRUE"]
  FN <- cm["TRUE", "FALSE"];  TP <- cm["TRUE", "TRUE"]
  precision <- ifelse(TP + FP == 0, 0, TP / (TP + FP))
  recall    <- ifelse(TP + FN == 0, 0, TP / (TP + FN))
  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold,
    Accuracy  = (TP + TN) / sum(cm),
    Precision = precision,
    Recall    = recall,
    F1_score  = ifelse(precision + recall == 0, 0,
                       2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall))
  )
}
```

**Original approach (exploratory).** The original script also tried a threshold of
**0.30**. That value was chosen *after looking at the test-set results*. Once the test
set has been used to choose a setting, it is no longer an independent check, so the
0.30 result is likely to be slightly optimistic.

**Revised approach (used for the final result).** The threshold is chosen using the
**training data only**: we try thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95 and keep the one with the
highest F1-score on the training sessions. The test set is then used **once** to
evaluate that choice.

```{r threshold-selection}
# Predicted probabilities for the TRAINING sessions
train_probabilities <- predict(model, newdata = train_data, type = "response")

# Try thresholds 0.05, 0.10, ..., 0.95 on the training data
threshold_grid <- round(seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05), 2)
train_scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(threshold_grid, function(t)
  get_metrics(train_probabilities, train_data$Revenue, t)))

best_threshold <- train_scores$Threshold[which.max(train_scores$F1_score)]
cat("Threshold with the highest training F1-score:", best_threshold, "\n")
```

```{r plot-threshold}
# Training-data precision, recall and F1-score at each threshold
threshold_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(Threshold = train_scores$Threshold, Metric = "Precision", Value = train_scores$Precision),
  data.frame(Threshold = train_scores$Threshold, Metric = "Recall",    Value = train_scores$Recall),
  data.frame(Threshold = train_scores$Threshold, Metric = "F1-score",  Value = train_scores$F1_score)
)

ggplot(threshold_long, aes(x = Threshold, y = Value, colour = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_threshold, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = best_threshold + 0.02, y = 0.05, hjust = 0,
           label = paste("chosen threshold =", best_threshold)) +
  labs(
    title = "Choosing the Threshold on the Training Data",
    x = "Classification Threshold",
    y = "Metric Value (training data)",
    colour = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** lowering the threshold raises recall (more buyers found) but lowers
precision (more false alarms). F1-score balances the two and is highest on the training
data at **`r best_threshold`**.

```{r evaluate-thresholds}
# Step 19 (extended): evaluate the thresholds on the TEST data
results <- rbind(
  cbind(Approach = "Original: standard threshold",          get_metrics(probabilities, test_data$Revenue, 0.50)),
  cbind(Approach = "Original: exploratory (chosen on test)", get_metrics(probabilities, test_data$Revenue, 0.30)),
  cbind(Approach = "Revised: chosen on training data",       get_metrics(probabilities, test_data$Revenue, best_threshold))
)
results_percent <- results
results_percent[, 3:6] <- round(100 * results_percent[, 3:6], 2)
results_percent

# Confusion matrix at the chosen threshold
final_predictions <- factor(ifelse(probabilities >= best_threshold, "TRUE", "FALSE"),
                            levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"))
final_cm <- table(Actual = actual_class, Predicted = final_predictions)
final_cm

# Save the results table (all values as proportions, 4 decimals)
results_to_save <- results
results_to_save[, 3:6] <- round(results_to_save[, 3:6], 4)
write.csv(results_to_save, "model_evaluation_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

All values above are percentages on the `r nrow(test_data)` test sessions.
`model_evaluation_results.csv` is saved in the project folder. It now also records
which threshold and approach each row belongs to; the original file stored only the
0.30 row.

## Prediction plot

```{r plot-predictions, fig.height = 4.8}
# Distribution of predicted purchase probabilities on the TEST data,
# shown separately for sessions that really did / did not end in a purchase.
plot_df <- data.frame(
  Probability = probabilities,
  Actual = ifelse(test_data$Revenue == "TRUE", "Actual: purchase", "Actual: no purchase")
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = Probability, fill = Actual)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.50, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_threshold, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ Actual, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Purchase Probability on the Test Data",
    subtitle = paste0("Dotted line: threshold 0.50   |   Dashed line: chosen threshold ", best_threshold),
    x = "Predicted Probability of Purchase",
    y = "Number of Sessions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Interpretation:** most non-purchase sessions receive probabilities close to 0, which
is why accuracy is high. Many real purchase sessions fall **between** the two lines;
moving the threshold from 0.50 down to `r best_threshold` turns these into correct
"purchase" predictions, which is why recall improves.

## Robustness checks *(added)*

Two checks test whether the conclusions depend on decisions made earlier. Each uses
the same steps as the main model: 80/20 split with `set.seed(123)`, threshold chosen on
training data, one evaluation on the test data.

```{r robustness}
# Re-runs the full procedure (split -> fit -> choose threshold on train -> test once)
run_procedure <- function(df, formula, label, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(df)), size = floor(0.8 * nrow(df)))
  tr <- df[idx, ]; te <- df[-idx, ]
  m  <- glm(formula, data = tr, family = binomial)
  p_tr <- predict(m, newdata = tr, type = "response")
  scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(threshold_grid, function(t) get_metrics(p_tr, tr$Revenue, t)))
  t_best <- scores$Threshold[which.max(scores$F1_score)]
  cbind(Model = label, get_metrics(predict(m, newdata = te, type = "response"), te$Revenue, t_best))
}

main_formula <- formula(model)

robustness <- rbind(
  run_procedure(data, main_formula, "Main model (duplicates kept)"),
  run_procedure(data[!duplicated(data), ], main_formula, "Duplicates removed"),
  run_procedure(data, update(main_formula, . ~ . - PageValues), "Without PageValues")
)
robustness[, 3:6] <- round(100 * robustness[, 3:6], 2)
robustness
```

A single split can move the numbers by a few points, depending on which sessions land
in the test set. To separate that effect from the duplicate decision, the full procedure
is repeated with 30 different random splits (seeds 1 to 30).

```{r repeated-splits, warning = FALSE}
# warning = FALSE: with a few of the 30 splits, glm() prints the message
# "fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred". This only means some sessions
# are predicted with near-certainty; it does not stop the model from fitting.
split_seeds <- 1:30
f1_kept    <- sapply(split_seeds, function(s)
  run_procedure(data, main_formula, "kept", seed = s)$F1_score)
f1_removed <- sapply(split_seeds, function(s)
  run_procedure(data[!duplicated(data), ], main_formula, "removed", seed = s)$F1_score)

repeated <- data.frame(
  Data = c("Duplicates kept", "Duplicates removed"),
  Mean_F1 = round(100 * c(mean(f1_kept), mean(f1_removed)), 2),
  Min_F1  = round(100 * c(min(f1_kept),  min(f1_removed)), 2),
  Max_F1  = round(100 * c(max(f1_kept),  max(f1_removed)), 2)
)
repeated
```

```{r pagevalues-check}
# Purchase rate for sessions with and without a positive PageValue
data %>%
  mutate(PageValues_group = ifelse(PageValues > 0, "PageValues > 0", "PageValues = 0")) %>%
  group_by(PageValues_group) %>%
  summarise(Sessions = n(), Purchase_Rate = round(mean(Revenue == "TRUE"), 4))
```

**Interpretation:**

* **Duplicates:** in the single split above, the F1-score is
  `r robustness$F1_score[1]`% with duplicates kept and `r robustness$F1_score[2]`% with
  them removed. Averaged over 30 different splits, the two are almost the same
  (`r repeated$Mean_F1[1]`% vs `r repeated$Mean_F1[2]`%). The gap in the single split
  therefore comes from *which sessions land in the test set*, not from the duplicates,
  and keeping them does not change the conclusions.
* **Split-to-split variation:** across the 30 splits, the main model's F1-score ranges
  from `r repeated$Min_F1[1]`% to `r repeated$Max_F1[1]`%. The reported result with
  `set.seed(123)` (`r robustness$F1_score[1]`%) lies inside this range, towards its
  lower end, so it is not an unusually lucky split.
* **PageValues:** without `PageValues`, the F1-score drops sharply, so this one variable
  carries most of the predictive power. Google Analytics calculates a page's value from
  purchases that happened after visitors viewed that page. The value may therefore
  partly reflect the purchase itself, and might not be fully known early in a session.
  The main model's results should be read as **an upper estimate** of what a real-time
  system could achieve.

# Results and Conclusion

## Key findings

* Only `r revenue_table$Percent[revenue_table$Revenue == "TRUE"]`% of
  `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` sessions end in a purchase; the data is imbalanced.
* Purchasing sessions have **lower bounce and exit rates** and much **higher page values**:
  `r round(100 * mean(data$Revenue[data$PageValues > 0] == "TRUE"), 1)`% of sessions with a
  positive page value end in a purchase, against
  `r round(100 * mean(data$Revenue[data$PageValues == 0] == "TRUE"), 1)`% of the rest.
* **New visitors** convert at a higher rate than returning visitors.
* The purchase rate varies by **month**, highest in
  `r as.character(month_summary$Month[which.max(month_summary$Purchase_Rate)])`.

## Model results (test data, `r nrow(test_data)` sessions)

```{r final-summary}
# Step 23: Final case study summary
final_row <- results[results$Approach == "Revised: chosen on training data", ]

cat("Total sessions:", nrow(data), "\n")
cat("Total variables:", ncol(data), "\n")
cat("Training sessions:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing sessions:", nrow(test_data), "\n")
cat("Chosen threshold (from training data):", best_threshold, "\n")
cat("Accuracy:",  round(final_row$Accuracy  * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Precision:", round(final_row$Precision * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("Recall:",    round(final_row$Recall    * 100, 2), "%\n")
cat("F1-score:",  round(final_row$F1_score  * 100, 2), "%\n")
```

With the threshold chosen on the training data, the Logistic Regression model reaches
an accuracy of `r round(100 * final_row$Accuracy, 2)`% and an F1-score of
`r round(100 * final_row$F1_score, 2)`% on unseen test sessions. It finds
`r round(100 * final_row$Recall, 1)`% of real purchases, compared with
`r round(100 * recall, 1)`% at the standard 0.50 threshold. This revised F1-score is very
close to the original exploratory result at 0.30
(`r round(100 * results$F1_score[2], 2)`%), which supports the decision to use a lower
threshold.

## Recommendations

1. **Reduce early exits.** High exit and bounce rates go with non-purchase; improving
   landing pages and navigation could keep more visitors in the session.
2. **Focus on high-value pages.** Sessions that reach pages with a positive page value
   are far more likely to buy; guide visitors towards these pages (product details,
   cart, offers).
3. **Win back returning visitors.** Returning visitors buy less often per session;
   reminders or personalised offers may raise their conversion.
4. **Plan by season.** Use the monthly differences to time campaigns and stock.

## Limitations

* **Threshold selection:** the final threshold is chosen on the training data, so it is
  slightly fitted to that data. A separate validation set or cross-validation would be
  stricter. The original 0.30 result was chosen on the test set and is exploratory only.
* **Single random split:** the main results come from one 80/20 split (`set.seed(123)`).
  Other splits give F1-scores between `r repeated$Min_F1[1]`% and `r repeated$Max_F1[1]`%
  (Section 5.8).
* **PageValues:** it may partly reflect the purchase itself (Section 5.8), so performance
  may be optimistic for real-time prediction.
* **Duplicates:** `r sum(duplicated(data))` identical rows were kept (Section 3.2); some of
  them fall into both the training and test sets.
* **Scope:** the data covers one year of one online store, so findings may not apply to
  other websites. Logistic Regression assumes a linear relationship on the log-odds
  scale and may miss more complex patterns.

## Conclusion

Session behaviour, especially page value, exit rate and visitor type, is clearly
associated with whether an online shopping session ends in a purchase. A simple,
interpretable Logistic Regression model built in R predicts purchases with high accuracy.
Choosing a lower threshold on the training data greatly improves how many buyers it
finds. All results in this report are produced by the R code above from the original
UCI dataset.
